title: What is known about 1RB1RE_1LC0RA_0RD1LB_---1RC_1LF1RE_0LB0LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RE_1LC0RA_0RD1LB_---1RC_1LF1RE_0LB0LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to a map on pairs of numbers. Lean proves (kernel, no native_decide) that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (2, 1) under the map f below reaches a pair with r = p + 1. Iterating the map 3,000,000 times, the orbit never does; by then p and r have about 650,000 binary digits, so the machine has run for more than 2650000 steps. A probability argument says a hit becomes ever less likely (the chance at each decision is about 1/p), so the machine is expected never to halt, but no proof is known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 28,376 cells have been visited and 19,729 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.074). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.483).

claims.title: The one-sweep rules
claims.text: With W p q r = 0 (10)^p 0 (10)^q 1^r E> 0 and X p q = 0 (10)^p 0 (10)^q A> 0 (the head at the right end): W (p+1) q (r+2) → W p (q+2) (r+1); W (p+1) q 1 → X p (q+2); X (p+1) (q+2) → W (p+1) 0 (2q+6); X 0 (q+2) → W 2 0 (2q+5); W 0 q (r+2) → W (q+2) 0 (r+1); W 0 q 1 halts. Each a theorem for all values, by symbolic simulation.

claims.title: The map
claims.text: Read at the samples W p 0 r (r ≥ 1): if r ≥ p+2 then (p, r) → (2p+2, r−p−1); if r = p+1 the machine halts; if r = p then (p, r) → (2, 4p+1); if r < p then (p, r) → (p−r, 4r+2). Each case is a positive run of the machine, chained from the rules by induction on the number of sweeps.

claims.title: Halts if and only if the orbit hits r = p + 1
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches W 2 0 1 in 27 steps; so it halts if and only if the orbit of (2, 1) under the map reaches a pair (p, p+1).

claims.title: The map matches the machine
claims.text: The 48 samples W p 0 r of the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps of the machine are exactly the first 48 points of the orbit of (2, 1).

claims.title: No halt in 3,000,000 map steps
claims.text: The orbit of (2, 1), iterated with exact integers, does not reach r = p+1 in its first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps; at the end p and r have about 650,000 bits. Each map step is at least one machine step and in fact at least p of them, so this covers far more than 2<sup>600000</sup> machine steps.

claims.title: Why a halt looks unlikely
claims.text: Halting can only happen when a doubling run ends: the last step leaves r somewhere in a range of about 2p values, and halting needs exactly r = p+1. Treating the leftover as random, the chance is about 1/(2p) per run; p grows exponentially (about 0.22 bits per map step), so the expected number of future hits is far below 2<sup>-100000</sup>. The closest approach in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps had |r−p−1|/p ≈ 3·10<sup>-6</sup>.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known: it halts exactly when the orbit of (2, 1) under the map reaches r = p+1, a question like a Collatz problem. No residue-class argument closes it (no modulus below 200 has an invariant set of residue pairs avoiding the halting pairs).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now about two numbers. This machine keeps three blocks on its tape; reading them at the right moments gives a pair (p, r), and Lean proves that the machine halts exactly when a simple map on such pairs, started at (2, 1), hits r = p + 1. The map has been iterated three million times without that happening.

facts.text: Lean: the machine halts iff the orbit of (2, 1) reaches a pair (p, p+1).
No hit; p has about 650,000 bits by then.
Chance of a hit at each decision; p doubles at most map steps.

sections.eyebrow: What the tape is made of
sections.heading: Three blocks
html: Whenever the head is at the right end of the tape, the tape reads

a block of p pairs 10, a separator, a block of q pairs, and a run of r ones. The head walks back and forth across the whole tape, so the right side grows like the square root of the time; the left end only moves when the left block runs out, which happens about once per doubling, so the left side grows like the logarithm of the time.

One sweep (right end → left block → right end) takes one pair from the left block, adds two pairs to the middle block and removes one 1: W (p+1) q (r+1) → W p (q+2) r. Sweeps repeat until one of the outer blocks is used up. Then:

• the left block runs out first (r ≥ p+2): the middle block, now 2p pairs, becomes the new left block with two more pairs, the tape growing one cell on the left: (p, r) → (2p+2, r−p−1);
  • the ones run out first (r < p): the middle block is turned into a run of ones, 4r+2 of them: (p, r) → (p−r, 4r+2);
  • both at once (r = p): everything is rebuilt as (2, 4p+1);
  • the left block runs out with exactly one 1 left (r = p+1): the head reaches state D on a blank cell, the halting transition.

sections.heading: A map on pairs
html:
f(p, r) = (2p+2, r−p−1)   if r ≥ p+2
          HALT              if r = p+1
          (2, 4p+1)         if r = p
          (p−r, 4r+2)       if r < p
From blank tape the first sample (27 steps) is (2, 1). The first points of the orbit, which match the machine's samples exactly:

Most steps are doublings (about 63%), the rest are resets r < p; the case r = p happened once, at the third step, and never again in three million steps. The quantity p + r goes up by one at each doubling and jumps at each reset, and both numbers grow by about 0.22 bits per step on average.

sections.heading: Halting means hitting r = p + 1 exactly
html: Lean proves the reduction both ways (halts_iff_orbit in lean/Map.lean, checked by the kernel): the machine halts from blank tape if and only if some point of the orbit of (2, 1) is a pair (p, p+1).

A run of doublings ends when r drops below p+2. Just before the last doubling r lies between p+2 and 3p+4 or so; after it, the leftover r is spread over about 2p values and halting needs one particular value. If the leftover behaves like a random number, the chance is about 1/(2p) at each decision, and since p grows exponentially the total chance left is astronomically small. That is the usual shape of a cryptid: almost certainly it runs forever, but proving it would mean controlling the digits of an orbit, as in the Collatz problem.
Checked: 3,000,000 steps of the map (p reaching about 650,000 bits) without a hit; the nearest miss had |r − p − 1| / p ≈ 3·10−6, about what chance predicts for the small values early on.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.074). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.483).
After 109 steps the tape spans 28,376 cells (68 left of the start, 21,792 right), with a density of 1s of 0.695.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A two-register map on (p, r): double p while r lasts, then reset; halts iff the orbit of (2, 1) hits r = p + 1 (proved in Lean). Not hit in 3·10^6 map steps.
